items.question: Why Anthropic?
lookFor: Two or three specific reasons, at least one tied to something you've read (RSP v3.x, Core Views) and hold a view on.
Connects to your own work: you built a production Claude platform and saw what safe deployment needs.
Avoids generic 'AI safety is important' or 'performing alignment'.
Honest about what you don't know yet.
followUps: What would make you leave Anthropic?
Which other AI companies did you consider, and why not them?

items.question: Why Forward Deployed Engineer rather than a pure engineering or sales role?
lookFor: Shows you understand the job: embedding with customers, building production artifacts (MCP servers, agents), and driving adoption.
Evidence from your 10+ years of technical customer work that you like being on site with customers.
Evidence from your AI platform that you can build, not only advise.
Names the part of the job you'll find hardest.
followUps: What part of the FDE job do you expect to find hardest?
How do you feel about 25-50% travel?

items.question: Which of our models have you used, and what did you build with them?
lookFor: Concrete: Claude API with tool use, batches and web search; an MCP server; research agents; approval steps and audit logs.
Explains why you chose specific features (e.g. batches for cost, tool use for system access) and model tradeoffs.
Mentions one limitation you hit and how you handled it.
Doesn't invent usage numbers you can't back up.
followUps: How did you decide which model to use where?
What broke first in production?
How did you know the outputs were good enough?

items.question: Give me your 60-second background.
lookFor: Arc in three beats: EPFL engineer -> 10+ years technical customer-facing (laser & additive manufacturing equipment, CH/CN/US) -> solo-built an internal Claude platform in production.
Ends with why that leads to this role.
Under 90 seconds; no CV recital.
followUps: Why did you move from equipment into AI?
What would your last customer say about you?

items.question: Walk me through one project you owned end to end. What were the hardest decisions?
lookFor: STAR plus architecture: problem -> constraints -> decisions and tradeoffs -> what broke -> metrics -> what you'd change.
Your own decisions, clearly separated from what others did.
Real numbers where you have them (users, time saved, error rates), honest where you don't.
Names a mistake, e.g. adding formal evals too late.
followUps: If you rebuilt it today, what would you change?
What did you decide not to build, and why?
How did you get people to actually use it?

items.question: You built your AI platform alone. Why n8n and Supabase instead of writing everything in code?
lookFor: Shows judgment: speed, maintainability by a small team, using what the company could support.
Acknowledges limits (testing, version control, scaling) and how you handled them.
Links to 'do the simple thing that works'.
followUps: When would you move off n8n?
How did you version and test workflows?
items.value: Do the simple thing that works

items.question: How did you evaluate whether your Claude workflows were good enough?
lookFor: Honest about what you did (spot checks, user feedback, approval-step data) and what you didn't (formal golden sets).
Describes what you'd do now: golden set from real cases, code graders where possible, calibrated LLM judge, regression on prompt changes.
No overclaiming.
followUps: What metric would you have tracked first?
How would you calibrate an LLM grader?

items.question: Tell me about a time your values were tested at work.
lookFor: A real situation with stakes (e.g. pressure to ship equipment or a workflow you knew wasn't ready).
What you did, what it cost you, and the outcome.
Honest reflection: what you'd do differently.
Link to an Anthropic value without forcing it.
followUps: Would you make the same call again?
How did the other person react?

items.question: What worries you about deploying powerful AI?
lookFor: A specific, reasoned worry (e.g. agents with write access acting on injected instructions, over-reliance by non-experts, misuse) rather than slogans.
Grounded in what you've seen in your own deployments.
Calibrated uncertainty; mentions both near-term and longer-term risks.
What you personally do about it (approval steps, audit logs, scope limits).
followUps: Which worry do you think is overrated?
How would you explain that risk to a customer?

items.question: What do you think of our Responsible Scaling Policy? Is there anything you disagree with?
lookFor: Knows the basics: capability thresholds trigger stronger safeguards (ASL levels); v3.x adds Frontier Safety Roadmaps and Risk Reports.
Gives one genuine opinion or open question, e.g. how external review via the Long-Term Benefit Trust works, or how a customer experiences classifiers.
Willing to disagree respectfully; doesn't just praise.
followUps: How would you explain ASL-3 safeguards to a customer who gets a false refusal?
What would make you lose trust in the RSP?
items.value: Ignite a race to the top on safety

items.question: Core Views describes optimistic, intermediate and pessimistic scenarios. Which do you find most likely, and why?
lookFor: Accurately describes the three scenarios.
Picks one with reasons and admits uncertainty.
Connects it to how Anthropic should act (empirical research, 'show, don't tell').
followUps: What evidence would change your mind?
What should Anthropic do if it became clear we're in the pessimistic case?

items.question: Tell me about a time you slowed down a launch for safety or quality reasons.
lookFor: Concrete stakes: customer pressure, revenue or timeline.
How you made the risk visible and proposed an alternative (smaller scope, pilot, extra test).
Result and what the relationship looked like afterwards.
followUps: Was anyone unhappy with you?
When is it right to ship anyway?

items.question: Tell me about a mistake you made that affected a customer or user.
lookFor: Takes ownership without excuses.
What you did immediately to limit damage and how you told the customer.
The systemic fix (process, check, guardrail), not only 'I'll be more careful'.
followUps: How did you find out?
What would have caught it earlier?

items.question: Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager or a senior colleague.
lookFor: Disagreed on substance with data, not ego.
How you raised it and listened to the other side.
Outcome, including if you were wrong; 'disagree and commit' if applicable.
followUps: What would you have done if they still said no?
Were you right in the end?

items.question: Tell me about a time you had to say 'I don't know' to a customer.
lookFor: Admits the gap in the moment instead of bluffing.
How you found the answer and followed up.
Why honesty kept the customer's trust.
followUps: Have you ever bluffed? What happened?
How do you prepare for questions you can't answer?

items.question: A customer asks you to build an agent with unrestricted write access to production systems 'to save time'. What do you do?
lookFor: Doesn't just refuse: understands the goal behind the request.
Proposes least-privilege tools, approval gates for irreversible actions, audit logs, staged rollout.
Explains the risk in the customer's terms (outage, data loss, compliance).
Knows when to escalate internally.
followUps: What if they insist and threaten to go to a competitor?
Which actions would you let run without approval?

items.question: Anthropic both builds frontier models and warns about their risks. How do you think about that tension?
lookFor: Understands the stated rationale: safety research needs frontier systems; influence on industry norms (race to the top).
Acknowledges the real tension and critiques of it.
States your own position honestly.
followUps: What would convince you Anthropic got the balance wrong?
How would you answer a customer who raises this?

items.question: Tell me about your most difficult customer and how you handled them.
lookFor: Specific customer situation (e.g. a machine failing acceptance tests abroad) with clear stakes.
How you separated the emotion from the technical problem and found the real issue.
Concrete actions and measurable outcome.
What you learned about managing expectations.
followUps: What would you do differently?
How did you keep your own team aligned?

items.question: Tell me about a time you told a customer 'no' or 'not yet'.
lookFor: The request, why it was wrong or risky (equipment limit, safety, quality).
How you said no while offering a path forward.
Outcome for the relationship and the deal.
followUps: Did you lose the deal?
How do you decide when to escalate instead of saying no yourself?

items.question: You built a great tool and nobody used it. Tell me how you've driven adoption.
lookFor: Real example from rolling out your platform to non-technical colleagues (e.g. via Teams).
Diagnosed why people didn't use it (trust, workflow fit, training) before pushing harder.
Specific tactics: champions, meeting users in their tools, quick wins, feedback loops.
Usage metric before and after.
followUps: Which group resisted most and why?
What did you stop building because of user feedback?

items.question: A customer executive says 'we need AI everywhere'. How do you turn that into something deliverable?
lookFor: Discovery first: business goals, current workflows, pain with numbers.
Prioritises by value x feasibility x risk; picks one narrow pilot with an eval set.
Sets expectations about what Claude can and can't do.
followUps: How do you handle a second executive with conflicting priorities?
What would make you walk away?

items.question: Tell me about a time you had to deliver bad news to a customer about a delay or limitation.
lookFor: Told early, with facts, without blaming others.
Brought options and a plan.
How trust changed afterwards.
followUps: How early did you know?
What did your company think of how you handled it?

items.question: You've worked with customers in Switzerland, China and the US. How did you adapt?
lookFor: Specific differences you observed (decision-making, directness, escalation).
One concrete example of adapting your approach.
Avoids stereotypes; focuses on listening.
followUps: When did you get it wrong?
How would that help you embed with a new customer team?

items.question: How would you bring customer feedback back to Anthropic's product and research teams?
lookFor: Recognises the FDE role includes spotting patterns across customers.
Structured feedback: problem, frequency, impact, workaround, evidence.
Example from your past of turning field feedback into a product change.
followUps: How would you prioritise one big customer's request vs a pattern across many?
What if product says no?
